en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
May the lotus-feet of Gaurī, made resonant by the bees that are the tresses of the Goddess of Immortality, dispel all misfortune. 1.
We praise the ancient husband and wife, the parents of the manifest world, who are each other’s fruit of the perfection of their mutual asceticism. 2.

May that Mukunda—who, having opened the calyx of the heart-lotus through the art of yoga, is grasped by the fortunate even from afar according to their desire, and who manifests incessantly in his full form—grant me eternal welfare. (3)
For the sake of enabling beginners to master the ornaments, this elegant compendium of their definitions and illustrations is now composed. (4)
Those for whom verses on definitions and defined terms are seen in the *Candrālikā* are mostly those [whose works are ancient];
for others, however, they are composed anew. ||5||
Upamā (simile) is that wherein the beauty of similarity between two things shines forth:
"O Kṛṣṇa! Like a female swan, your fame plunges into the celestial Gaṅgā. (6)

Where the beautiful similarity between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) shines forth, manifesting clearly without the boundaries of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), and thereby delighting the hearts of the connoisseurs, there exists the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). An example is "like a female swan" (*haṃsīva*). This is called a "complete simile" (*pūrṇopamā*) because all four elements—the standard of comparison, the object of comparison, the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the comparison (*upamāvācaka*)—are present; namely, the female swan, the fame (*kīrti*), the act of plunging into the celestial Gaṅgā, and the word "like" (*iva*). [As it is said: "The wise man perceives merits and defects as the Lord [perceives] the moon and poison."

"First he is praised with his head, but finally he is held in the throat. Here, although there is no single common attribute for the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameya)—for while both the moon and the poison are grasped (i.e., mentioned) in the case of the Lord (the upamāna), it is the former of these two, the moon, that is praised with the head—

The distinction [between this and the previous type] is that [in the former] there is a welcoming through a nod of the head, the restraint of the subsequent fault at the throat, and the non-utterance of words above the throat. Nevertheless, because the moon and the poison stand in the relation of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), and because there is a determination of identity through the employment of the single word *gṛhyann* (being seized) which applies to both the material cause and the cognition, they constitute a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*); this is the distinction from the previous case.

According to the established doctrine of the Alaṅkārikas, the "relation of the original image and its reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) consists in the separate mention of two attributes belonging to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), which are in fact distinct but appear as non-distinct due to their mutual similarity. ||6||

The elliptical simile (luptopamā) is divided into eight types based on the omission of one, two, or three of the following: the object of description (varṇya), the standard of comparison (upamāna), the common attribute (dharma), and the word expressing comparison (upamāvācaka). ||7||
In secret, I beheld that slender woman, white as lightning, her face like the moon, filling my eyes with camphor-like purity, and through her radiance appearing like the bride of Love. (8)
That meeting with her, and the gain I have from my devotion to her—that is all a "crow-and-palmyra" occurrence, arising without prior deliberation. (9)

Among the four elements—the object of comparison (*upameya*) and so forth—it is called an *elided simile* (*luptopamā*) when there is an absence of the expressive word for one, two, or three of them. It is of eight kinds: namely, elision of the expresser (*vācakaluptā*), elision of the attribute (*dharmaluptā*), elision of both attribute and expresser (*dharmavācakaluptā*), elision of the expresser and the object of comparison (*vācalopameyaluptā*), elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*), elision of the expresser and the standard of comparison (*vācakopamānaluptā*), elision of the attribute and the standard of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*), and elision of the attribute, the standard of comparison, and the expresser (*dharmopamānavācakaluptā*). Among these, the four varieties that exclude the elision of the standard of comparison have been illustrated by the verse beginning with "taḍidgaurī."

The various types [of ellipsis] possessing those [features] are shown by the following verse. Among them, in the example "taḍidgaurī" (lightning-white), there is an elision of the *vācaka* (the expressive word); this occurs by virtue of the rule prescribing the compound, namely "upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ" (comparisons with words expressing common properties). In the example "indutulyāsyā" (her face is like the moon), there is an elision of the *dharma* (the common property); however, this is optional and not mandated by the rule, since one could equally say "kāntyā indutulyāsyā" (her face is like the moon in its brilliance).

In the expression "karpūrantī," there is an elision of the word denoting the quality (*dharma-vācaka-lopa*). This occurs because the *kip* suffix—which is prescribed in the sense of "acting like camphor" (*karpūram ivācarantī*) to signify an action characterized by bliss—is elided along with the word *iva*. Here, the elision of the quality is optional (*aicchika*), for since both [the woman and camphor] consist of bliss, the inclusion of that [quality] would also be possible, as in the form "karpūrantī."

In the verse "kāntyā smaravadhūyantī," there is an elision of both the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). Here, by the power of the qualifier "by her beauty" (*kāntyā*), the sense that "she acts like the wife of Kāma toward herself" is implied; thus, because the object of comparison—her own self—is not mentioned along with the word expressing the simile, this [elision] is optional (*aicchika*), since it is also possible to mention the object of comparison as in "acting like the wife of Kāma toward herself."

In the expression *kākatālīya*, the words *kāka* (crow) and *tāla* (palmyra tree) refer, within the context of the compound formation (*vṛtti*), to the actions inherent in the crow and the palmyra tree respectively. Thus, by the rule "and [the suffix *cha*] after a compound whose object is that [action]" (*samāsācca tadviṣayāt*), a compound is formed in the sense of "like the crow's arrival" and "like the falling of the palmyra fruit" (*kākatālam iva*). In both cases, the object of comparison is one's own departure to a certain place and the secret presence of the slender maiden right there. Consequently, it results that the meeting between oneself and her is similar to the meeting of the crow and the palmyra fruit.

Then, regarding the expression *kākatāliya* (meaning "like the case of the crow and the palm fruit"), the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt*, which falls under the governing heading *ive pratikṛtau*. Thus, just as a palm fruit, split by falling, was consumed by a crow, so too was the slender maiden, her heart agitated by the sight of him in secret. Because the object of comparison (*upamāna*)—namely, the act of consuming the palm fruit—is not explicitly mentioned, there is an elision of the object of comparison in a derivative-based simile (*pratyayārthopamā*), or an elision of the expressive object of comparison in a compound-based simile (*samāsārthopamā*).

All this elision is produced by the rules prescribing the suffix *cha*; it has been determined through subtle observation that when the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not mentioned because its occurrence was not considered possible, there is an elision of both the attribute and the object of comparison in a simile based on a suffix (*pratyayārthopamā*); whereas in a simile based on a compound (*samāsārthopamā*), there is an elision of the words expressing the attribute and the object of comparison. Other examples of these have not been written here for fear of prolixity. (7–9)
When a single object itself possesses the status of both the standard of comparison and the object compared—as in "The moon is like the moon, glorious"—that is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence). ||10||

The description of a single object as both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence). This follows from the etymological derivation that even when being described, its own similarity with itself does not correspond. The expression of a non-corresponding object is for the purpose of highlighting its incomparability by excluding other similar things. When it is said, "The moon is like the moon in splendor," the exclusion of other similar things is implied, signifying that there is no other thing equal to the moon in its splendor.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for anything to be similar to itself, this results in the absence of any object of comparison (*anupameyatva*). As it is said: "The sky is like the sky; the ocean is like the ocean; the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa."
In the previous example, there was the inclusion of the property of "possessing glory" (śrīmattva);
here, however, the distinction is that in [the case of] space and so forth, there is no such inclusion of the property of "vastness" (vaipulya) and the like. ||10||
If that same [similarity] occurs between two things by way of exchange, it is considered *upameyopamā* (the comparison of the object compared):
"In you, Dharma is like Artha in its full glory, and Artha is like Dharma. (11)

The conceptualization of two things as being alternately the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameya) is for the purpose of excluding a third similar entity. For when the similarity of one thing to another regarding either dharma or artha is described, the similarity of that [second thing] to yet another is established by implication; however, when it is explicitly described, it results in the exclusion of a third similar entity. As in: "The sky is like the water, the water is like the sky; the swan is like the moon, the moon is like the swan; the stars have the form of white water-lilies, and the white water-lilies have the form of stars."

In the previous instance, the quality of "fullness" (*pūrṇaśrī*) was employed; here, qualities such as "stainlessness" (*nirmalatva*) are not employed—this is the distinction. In both examples, the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is conceived between two things that are themselves the subject matter (*prakṛta*). Since the abundance of virtue and wealth in the king and the stainlessness of the sky and water in autumn are both the subjects of description, this figure can also occur between a subject and a non-subject (*prakṛtāprakṛta*). For example: "This king-elephant shines like a mountain, and the mountain shines loftily like a king-elephant.
A stream of ichor flows like a waterfall, and a waterfall flows from him like a stream of ichor. (11)
The inverse simile consists in the conceptualization of the standard of comparison as the object of comparison:
"The lotus is equal to your eye; the moon is similar to your face. (12)
*Pratīpa* (the inverse) occurs when the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), which is well-established, is reversed.
For example:

"O beloved! That blue lotus which possesses a luster equal to your eyes is submerged in the water; the moon, which imitates the beauty of your face, is hidden by clouds; and those royal swans whose gait follows yours have departed. Fate does not permit even a mere diversion through your likeness to me. (12)
And that [is] the disregard for the subject of description (varṇya) due to the acquisition of another object of comparison:
"Enough with your pride, O face! Even the moon is like that in its radiance. (13)

When an object being described as possessing exceedingly superior qualities cannot tolerate its similarity to anything else, and some other object is shown as a point of comparison only to be surpassed by it—that is the second type of *pratīpa* (the inverse), which possesses a distinct charm even greater than the first. For example: "O fair lady, why do you carry this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes? Surely such blue lotuses exist in every direction within the lakes! (13)
Likewise, by attaining the status of the subject of description and the object of comparison, there is disregard for others as well:
"O Death! What pride do you have in your cruelty? For there are women who are equal to you. (14)

The third type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) occurs when the subject of description (*avarṇya*), being possessed of such exceedingly superior qualities that it cannot endure even the slightest state of being compared to anything else, is imagined to have the object of description (*varṇya*) as its own point of comparison; by this means, the latter is disparaged. This stands in contrast to the previously mentioned *pratīpa*. For example: "O Hālāhala [poison], my dear father! Do not be so arrogant, thinking, 'I alone am the teacher of all things most cruel. Are there not, indeed, many more words like yours in this world belonging to wicked men? (14)
And that statement regarding the impossibility of comparing one thing to another by means of its quality—"O lovely-eyed one, the lotus is indeed said to resemble your face"—is a vain reproach. (15)

The fourth type of *pratīpa* (the inverse), which possesses excellence over previous types, consists of the statement that the comparison is not established because the object of comparison (*upameya*) is not worthy of being compared. In the example, the non-establishment of the comparison is revealed by the mention of joy (*mudā*) as a ground for censure (*apavāda*). Or, for instance: "Listen, O lotus-eyed one, to this reproach on earth:
the moon is compared to your face by the vulgar. (15)
They also consider the purposelessness of the standard of comparison when it is contrary [to the fact];
for instance: "If her face has been seen, what is the use of the lotus, or what is the use of the moon? (16)

The fifth type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) arises from the futility of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because it serves as the primary vehicle for the purpose of the subject of comparison (*upameya*) itself; this occurs through a contradiction with the standard of comparison. For example: "Whenever [the sun] forms the thought in its mind, 'These two [the moon and the sun] exist in vain compared to his power and his fame,' then Fate, under the pretext of a halo around the sun, subjects even the moon to the state of being circled [by a ring of light]. Some consider *ananvaya*, *upameyopamā*, and *pratīpa* to be specific varieties of *upamā* (simile) and thus include them within that category.
Others, however, call the fifth type of *pratīpa* the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), because it consists in the negation of the standard of comparison. (16)
Metaphor (rūpaka) consists in the coloring of the object (viṣaya) by means of its identity with the subject (viṣayin);
it is of three kinds, according to the expression of superiority, inferiority, or neither. ||17||
For this is Dhūrjaṭi himself, by whom the cities were burnt in an instant;
yet here he remains without Śambhu’s third eye. (18)
Today Śambhu protects the universe by embracing equanimity; now that the delight of his eyes has been obtained through her moon-like face, what need is there for the [celestial] moon? 19.
This other virtuous Lakṣmī has arisen from the ocean of nectar;
this moon of a face surpasses the spotless moon. (20)

The *viṣayin* (the possessor of the form) is the object of comparison, such as a lotus; the *viṣaya* (the object) is that which is being compared, such as the face, which is the subject of description. *Rūpaka* (metaphor) is the coloring of the *viṣaya* by means of the form of the *viṣayin*, because it effects the possession of the form of one thing by another. This [metaphor] in some cases culminates in the non-difference (*abheda*) of the well-known *viṣayin*, while in other cases it culminates merely in the superimposition (*āropa*) of its attributes, even though difference remains perceived. Consequently, *rūpaka* is of two kinds: *abhedarūpaka* (metaphor of non-difference) and *tādūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of identity).

Each of these two types is further threefold: by describing the excellence of the well-known object, by describing its inferiority, and by stating neither. Thus, this metaphor (*rūpaka*) is of six kinds. The *abhedopacāra* (metaphors based on non-difference) are illustrated by the one and a half verses beginning with "For this... (*ayaṃ hi*), and the *tādūpyarūpaka* (metaphors of identity) are illustrated by the one and a half verses beginning with "By her moon-like face" (*asyā mukhendunā*). These have been exemplified in the reverse order of their enumeration—namely, by the statement of excellence, inferiority, and neither.

By the qualifying phrase "by whom [the enemy] was burnt," there is an identification with the well-known Śiva superimposed upon the king who is being described; because no deficiency or superiority is described regarding Śiva’s state in his previous condition versus the state of the king being described, this is the first type: *Abhedarūpaka* (Metaphor of Non-difference) that is neither of the two [deficiency or superiority]. By the mention of the loss of the third eye, a deficiency relative to the previous state is demonstrated; thus, this is the second type: *Nyūnābhedarūpaka* (Metaphor of Deficient Non-difference). Even this description of deficiency is striking, as it serves to strengthen the sense of identity.

The third is the *adhikābhyasvarūpaka* (superlative metaphor), because by stating that Śiva is the protector of the world through the abandonment of partial vision (*viṣamadṛṣṭi*), his excellence in the state of being Rāhu is manifested compared to his previous state. In this way, in the subsequent examples of *tādrūpyarūpaka*, the states of neither, inferior, and superior should be inferred in order. Following this very sequence, here are other examples: "On this sandy bank of the Śarayū, its sands made bright by the moonlight, a game of dice was played for a long time by two Siddha youths."

One says that Kaiṭabha was slain first; another says Kaṃsa. "Tell me the truth, O Blessed One! Who was killed there first? Here, by the words "you yourself" (*sa tvam*), the identity between the speaker and the one who slew both Kaṃsa and Kaiṭabha is established through the pretext of questioning their chronological order; because this strengthens their essential oneness and prevents any perception of superiority or inferiority between the former state and the present, this is an *anubhayābheda-rūpaka* (a metaphor of non-difference between neither). "The Creator has created a twofold delusion regarding beautiful women and gold."

Unattached even to those [pleasures], He is Bharga Himself in human form. Here, by the qualifier "sākṣāt" (directly/manifest), His identity with Śiva—well-known as the one who is detached—is shown; yet, by the phrase "narākṛtiḥ" (human form), there is a metaphor of "inferior non-difference," which establishes the absence of a divine physical form. When you arrived, why did this ocean tremble? Since you are the maker of the bridge and the churning-staff, does it fear you? Indeed, even in another continent, there is no one subject to your will today; O bull among kings, Lakṣmī herself attends upon you.

Here, by stating the identity between the subject of description and Puruṣottama—the agent of both the bridge and the churning through the words "you, the maker of the bridge and the churner"—it is implied that nevertheless, the ocean need not fear whether his arrival is for the purpose of building a bridge or for the purpose of churning.

Since even other continents have come under your subjection, as before there are no more continents to be conquered and since you have already attained sovereign fortune, there is no occasion for further churning; thus, by perceiving an excellence over the previous state, this is an *adhikābhedopamā* (metaphor of superlative identity). Does it not destroy the lotus? Does it not bestow joy upon the eyes? Or does it not cause the increase of the fish-bannered god [Kāma] merely by its appearance?

"While this other cool-rayed moon (the second moon) shines upon your moon-like face, there might be pride [on its part] if it were due to nectar; yet even that exists indeed in your bimba-red lip. Here, by the phrase "another cool-rayed moon," the distinction of the moon of the face from the well-known [celestial] moon is revealed; and by establishing merely that it performs the functions of the well-known moon, neither superiority nor inferiority is expressed. Thus, this is the *tādrūpya-śleṣopamā* (metaphor based on identity through punning). "Brahmā is not four-faced; Hari is another who has but two arms..."

The Lord Śambhu is without an eye on his forehead, and the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa has four faces. Here, because of the qualifying term "another" (*apara*) applied to Hari and the others, it is made clear that the intention is to express their identity with [the respective deities] in all three cases; yet, since the deficiency of having only three faces and so forth is stated, this is a *nyūnatādūpyopamā* (metaphor of deficient identity). According to the opinion of Vāmana, this is an example of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). As he says: "When there is the conceptualization of the loss of one quality, the firmness of the equality of qualities is *viśeṣokti*. "O dull-witted one, do you think that the mind of Bhīma’s daughter should sink into me while these life-breaths of hers are wasting away?"

The god of love, Smara, declared that my ear was intended for that [Vedic] meaning which refers to the moon-like face of Nala. In this instance, regarding Damayantī’s reproach of the moon, the well-known celestial moon is not the intended object of the Vedic passage concerning the entry into the mind at the time of departure; rather, it is the moon of Nala’s face. Because this establishes his superiority over the former, it is an *adhikatād rūpya* (metaphor of superior resemblance). The detailed exposition of the divisions of metaphor, such as those with and without parts (*sāvayava* and *niravayava*), should be sought in the *Citramīmāṃsā*. (17–20)
If transformation is for the sake of action, then the subject, by means of the object's nature, gazes with her clear lotus-eye upon the one with intoxicating eyes. 21.

The figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation) occurs where the superimposed object (*viṣayin*), being employed for the sake of some specific purpose, requires transformation into its own original form because it cannot naturally serve that purpose; an example of this is the verse beginning with "prasanna... (clear...). For here, the utility of the lotus (*abja*) for the act of seeing is established, but not that of the eye (*dṛś*). This is because, in compounds such as *mayūravyaṃsaka*, the meaning of the final member is predominant.

Nor should it be argued that, by resorting to an *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), there is primacy of the first member of the compound as in the expression "the eye-lotus" (*dṛgabjam iva*). This is because the word "clear" (*prasanna*) is employed as a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*). For the rule "that which is compared with tigers and the like [forms a compound] when the common attribute is not used" prescribes the *upamita-samāsa* only when such an attribute is absent. Furthermore, the utility of a lotus for the act of seeing is not possible in its own right; therefore, since it requires transformation into the nature of the subject at hand—the eye—it constitutes the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).

Or rather, having himself crossed the river of the gods—the garland upon the head of the Lord of Beings—he provided a boat made of his friendship for the son of Sumitrā to the ferryman. Then, followed with difficulty by Śabara maidens whose breasts were graspable within the span of their arms and whose eyes were upturned in curiosity, he set out for a moment toward Mount Citrakūṭa.

In this context, the brother being superimposed [upon Guha] is useful for the purpose of the effect—characterized by the assistance rendered to Guha—by way of his affectionate nature toward the son of Sumitrā, and not in his own right; for Guha’s sole aim was the favor of the Lord of the Raghus, and thus he had no desire for wages. ||21||
The description of a single object by many people in various ways is called *ullekha* (multiple description).
He was perceived as the God of Love by women, as the celestial tree by supplicants, and as Time by his enemies. (22)

When a single object, though capable of possessing various attributes, is depicted in multiple ways by different perceivers due to the diversity of the causes consisting in its connection with those respective attributes, that is *ullekha* (multiple depiction). In this multiple depiction, preference, desire, fear, and so forth serve as the respective motivating factors. Preference (*ruci*) is delight; desire (*arthitva*) is the wish to obtain.

The verse beginning with "By women" (*strībhiḥ*) provides an example of this: because he alone was a king endowed with the prowess of bestowing beauty, he was seen by women—as well as by supplicants and adversaries who were driven by desire, longing, and fear—as the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree of love and Time itself. Or, for instance, Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) was seen with curiosity by old women as a "savior of elephants," by young women as the "beloved of Śrī," and by children exactly as he was.

Here, he who swiftly rescued the elephant Bhīta when it was thus terrified is this very Supreme Puruṣottama; thus was Kṛṣṇa seen by the elderly women of Mathurā city as he entered, for they, fearing the cycle of worldly existence, sought his protection from fear. And he who is the eternal beloved of even Śrī, renowned for her fickleness, through his skill in the arts of love, is this very Divine Youth; thus was he seen with longing by the throngs of young women.

However, by the young women—who were solely intent on beholding his external appearance, dress, and ornaments—he was seen as being endowed with his usual attire and so forth; thus, there is a manifold representation. The former [example] was mixed with *rūpaka* (metaphor) due to the superimposition of the nature of Kāma and so on, whereas this one is pure (*śuddha*); such is the distinction. ||22||
Even when many descriptions are given by a single person, he appears different according to the distinction of the subject matter:
he is a preceptor in speech, Arjuna in fame, and Bhīṣma in the wielding of the bow.
Even in the absence of a difference among perceivers, this "multiple description" (*ullekha*) arises from the description of many aspects due to the difference in objects.

An example mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows: [The phrase] "greatly skilled in the matter of speech" (*vacoviṣaye mahān paṭuḥ*), which includes other meanings such as "Bṛhaspati" (the preceptor of the gods). A pure example is as follows: "May the fortune of the Skull-Bearer (Śiva) manifest: not meager in his breasts, slender at the waist, vast in his eyes, broad in his hips, ruddy in his lip, and full of compassion in his heart. (23)
Through memory, error, and doubt, there are three ornaments for that [suggestion]:
"As I gaze at the lotus, my mind plunges into the face of my beloved. (24)
This intoxicated bee thinks your face is a lotus, or the moon thinks a lotus is nectar; as for us, however, there is no certainty.

When [an object] is described through memory, error, or doubt based on similarity, there arise three ornaments marked by the terms "memory" (*smṛti*) and so forth—namely, *Smṛti*, *Bhrāntimān*, and *Saṃdeha*. These have been illustrated in sequence. Or, for example: "Beholding before him a certain woman emerging like the Goddess Śrī, with hands as beautiful as shimmering lotuses, who caused even the gods to marvel, Śauri (Viṣṇu) recalled the churning of the ocean."

In the previous example involving recollection (*smṛtimat*), there was the recollection of only a similar object; here, however, following the recollection of a similar beauty, there is also the recollection of its related event, the churning of the ocean—this is the distinction. "The bee falls upon the parrot’s beak, mistaking it for a *palāśa* bud; that [beak] too desires to seize the bee, mistaking it for a *jambū* fruit. Here, the distinction from the previous example lies in the basis of mutual delusion regarding each other's objects. "Bending when grasped while alive, they become upright again once they have been seized."

How much more so, then, are wicked people the "uppermost wheel" of the water-wheel? The distinction is that while the previously cited doubt has a well-known alternative (prasiddhakoṭika), this one has an imagined alternative (kalpitakoṭika). ||24-25||
Pure Apahnuti (pure concealment) is the denial of a quality for the purpose of superimposing another;
"This is not the moon, but rather a lotus of the celestial Ganges. (26)

*Śuddhāpahnuti* (pure concealment) is the denial of the attributes of an object under description, resulting in the superimposition of attributes similar to them; it is also the denial of other attributes imagined through the poet’s creative fancy. For example, in the case of the moon, there is the denial of its attribute of "moon-ness," resulting in the superimposition of the status of being a "white lotus of the celestial river. Or, for example: "Some suspected it was a rabbit; others considered it the mud of the ocean; some declared it a deer; and others maintained it was the shadow of the earth."

That which is seen at night in the moon, dark as a fragment of split sapphire, we declare to be the thick, swallowed-up darkness residing within its belly. Here, although the attributes of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) are present, their negation is established by implication through the presentation of an alternative view. ||26||
If that same [denial] is expressed by means of reasoning, it is called *hetvapahnuti* (denial through a reason):
"The moon is not intense; nor is the sun at night; this is the submarine fire risen from the ocean. (27)

In this instance, by means of the reasons of intensity and nocturnality, the very nature of being the moon and the sun is negated for the sake of superimposing the nature of the submarine fire upon the moon. Or, as in: "The scar of the wound from the friction of thousands of mountain-root-rocks against the churning-stick earth remains throbbing in the center of the moon; the 'shadow-deer' and the 'hare' are merely the talk of the vulgar, for there is no possibility whatsoever of those things existing there."

In this context, since there is no possibility of shadows and the like arising from a scar caused by the impact of the Mandara mountain during the time of churning within the moon, the denial of its being a shadow and so forth is revealed by citing the words of a common person. ||27||
Elsewhere, however, it serves the purpose of superimposition; that is *paryastāpahnuti* (the denial by inversion). ||28||

*Paryastāpahnuti* (Inverted Concealment) occurs when there is a denial of a particular attribute in one object for the purpose of superimposing that same attribute upon another object intended to be described. For example, the concealment of "moon-ness" in the moon for the purpose of superimposing it upon the face, which is the object to be described. Or, as in: "Hālāhala is not poison; poison is Ramā. People consider this a complete reversal. Having drunk it, Śiva remains awake in comfort; touching her, Hari faints away in sleep. In this case, the nature of poison is denied in Hālāhala and attributed to Ramā, while the nature of Ramā is denied in her and attributed to Hālāhala. This inversion of attributes constitutes *paryastāpahnuti*.

The distinction here is that while there was no statement of a reason in the previous example, there is one here. Consequently, as in the previous case of *apahnuti*, two varieties should be observed here as well. ||28||
**Concealment by Mistake:** When there is a suspicion of something else, this [figure] serves to ward off that mistake.
"O fever, why do you cause such burning accompanied by trembling? "No, my friend, it is not fever; it is Love. (29)

In this context, when the state of Smara (the God of Love) has been described as "he causes torment here," and a friend of straightforward intellect asks, "Is it fever? because of its similarity to fever, the confusion is dispelled by the statement of truth: "No, my friend! It is Smara. Or, for example: "O city-dweller! What is this buffalo here with such great height and a tail on both sides? No, no; this is a young elephant; this is his trunk, not a tail."

This is an example of *bhrāntāpahnuti* (concealment by delusion) preceded by an actual delusion. An example of that preceded by an imagined delusion (*kalpitabhrāntipūrvā*) is as follows: "This is not matted hair; it is merely a mass of hair fashioned into a braid. This is not poison in the throat; it is musk. This is not a crescent moon on the head; it is a flower. This is not ash upon the body; it is the whiteness born of separation from my beloved. O Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma)! Why do you strike me under the mistaken impression that I am Śiva? In this instance, the imagined delusion is to be inferred solely from the negations such as "this is not matted hair," because, as in the previous case, there is no question [of doubt].

Daṇḍin, however, considered this to be a variety of simile called *tattvākhyānopamā* (simile by way of stating the true nature). As he said: "‘This is not a lotus; it is indeed a face. These are not two bees; they are these two eyes’—because of the clearly manifest similarity, that is precisely a *tattvākhyānopamā*. (29)
Thus ends the figure of speech *chekāpahnuti* (clever denial), which occurs when there is a denial of a reality due to a suspicion of something else:
"Is it my beloved who is clinging to my feet while speaking? No, it is merely an anklet. (30)

*Chekāpahnuti* (Artful Concealment) occurs when, upon someone else overhearing a secret spoken by one person to another, the speaker conceals the truth by describing a different intention for their own words. For example, when a heroine’s playful companion is recounting her own lover’s conduct—saying, "He spoke while clinging to my foot"—another woman, hearing this, becomes suspicious and asks, "Is it your lover? To which she replies in concealment, "No, it is my anklet. [The verse continues: "It teaches the sound *sīt*, it wounds the lower lip, and it spreads horripilation."

"A citizen? What, has a citizen arrived? "No, no, my friend! It is the winter breeze. This is an example of the concealment of truth through the application of meaning (*arthayojanā*). As for the application of words (*śabdayojanā*), consider this: "O Padmā! I constantly remember your eyes; my heart faints at your dark tresses. What shall I do? I am captivated by your charms! Hearing these words spoken in a dream, Kṛṣṇa was rebuked with anger by Rādhā. May that playful lover, who then sought to justify those very words as referring to something else, protect you!

All of this is an illustration regarding the application [of a word] to a different object. Even when the object is the same, as in the case of application through a difference in state, for example: A cunning woman, relating the conduct of her lover to her husband under the guise of a friend, completed her sentence upon realizing it was her husband: "Friend! Since then, I have been awake. (30)
Disguised Denial (kaitavāpahnuti) occurs when there is a concealment through words such as "pretext" (vyāja) and the like, once the [true nature] has been revealed:
"The arrows of Love emerge under the pretext of the glances cast by my beloved. (31)

Here, by the word "deception" (*kaitava*), which expresses their unreality, there is understood the *apahnuti* (concealment) that these are not the side-long glances of beloved women, but rather "the arrows of Love. Or, for example: "In the depths of the forest, parched by the heat of the great midday sun expanding at noon, the trees—with tongues protruding under the guise of the flames of forest fires rising from their trunks—beg for water. (31)
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consists in a supposition (*saṃbhāvanā*) [of one thing as another] through the nature of a thing, a cause, or an effect;
it is either expressed or unexpressed, and its locus is either established or unestablished, the latter being the other type. (32)
Smoke, water, darkness, the moon, and the heat of the cakravāka birds' separation—darkness seems to smear the limbs, and the sky seems to rain down collyrium. (33)
Your two feet are certainly soft and red from being cast upon the ground;
surely, out of a desire for the splendor of your face, the moon is made to act as a rival by the lotuses.
Is his waist bound with golden chains for the sake of supporting his breasts?
For he seems to be performing penance in the water to attain oneness with your lotus-like feet.

*Utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is the imagining of one thing as being identical with another, based on the connection with some other attribute. It is threefold, according to whether its object is a thing (*vastu*), a cause (*hetu*), or an effect (*phala*). Among these, the first—where there is the imagining of a certain thing as being identical with another thing—is called *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential nature). The imagining of what is not a cause as having the state of a cause, or of what is not an effect as having the state of an effect, is called *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy regarding the cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the effect). Of these, the first type, *svarūpotprekṣā*, is twofold: that whose subject is expressed (*uktaviṣayā*) and that whose subject is unexpressed (*anuktaviṣayā*).

The other [types of] *utprekṣā*—those based on cause (*hetu*) and fruit (*phala*)—are each twofold: having a proven subject (*siddhaviṣayā*) and having an unproven subject (*asiddhaviṣayā*). Thus, there are six types of *utprekṣā*, with "the mass of smoke" (*dhūmastoma*) and so forth serving as their respective examples in order. In the example beginning with "at the onset of night," the darkness spreading everywhere possesses attributes such as blueness and the obstruction of vision; by means of this implied motive (*nimitta*), there arises a conceptual identification (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*) between the darkness—the object (*viṣaya*)—and the mass of smoke from the fires of separation about to blaze up in the hearts of the female *kokila* birds whose mates have suddenly departed for all parts of the world. This is an *svarūpotprekṣā* (intrinsic *utprekṣā*), and because the object, namely the darkness, is explicitly mentioned, it is an *uktaviṣayā* (explicitly stated subject).

There is a metaphorical identification (*tādātmyotprekṣā*) of darkness as the agent of smearing, based on the cause of its pervading all objects from the sky down to the earth by making them densely soiled; and there is also a metaphorical identification of the sky as the agent of raining collyrium, which is a metaphorical identification (*svarūpotprekṣā*) whose object is unstated, because in both cases the object of the pervasion—the darkness—is not explicitly mentioned.

[Objection: "In this case, let there be two metaphors (utprekṣā)—one based on the cause of darkness spreading [over the sky], which consists in the identification with the agent of smearing, and another based on the cause of the sky being pervaded by intense blackness up to the earth's horizon, which consists in the identification with the agent of raining collyrium; thus, both metaphors would have the aforementioned as their objects. [Reply:

Not so. Although the verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) in *limpati* ("smears") and *varṣati* ("rains") denote the agent, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verb has the action as its primary meaning," the action expressed by the verbal root is indeed primary. Since the agent is construed as subordinate to that action, it must itself be the object of the metaphor; therefore, it is impossible for it to be construed elsewhere [as the substratum]. For this very reason:

[Because the agent, who is the meaning of the verbal suffix, cannot be construed elsewhere since he is subordinate to the action,] Daṇḍin has also rejected the possibility of this [agent] being construed as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in a simile, stating: "If the agent were the standard of comparison, he would be subordinated to the word denoting the action; being occupied with accomplishing his own action, he is not capable of looking toward another. However, some say that there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential properties of the objects—darkness and the sky—namely, their being smeared and rained upon by that [agent].

In his view, it should be understood that there are only two types of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature itself): namely, *svarūpotprekṣā* and *dharmyutprekṣā*. Since the redness of the two feet is self-established, casting them aside (*vikṣepaṇa*) is not actually its cause; therefore, the fancy of imagining that non-cause as a cause is *hetūtprekṣā*. Because the object (*viṣaya*), namely the act of casting aside, exists, it is a *siddhaviṣayā* (one whose object is established).

Since the moon’s natural opposition to the lotus is not caused by its desire to attain the splendor of the heroine’s face, the attribution of causality to that desire constitutes *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of cause); because such a desire does not exist in reality, it is a case where the object [of the fancy] is unestablished (*asiddhaviṣayā*). In the case of the middle [part of the body], it holds the breasts of its own accord, and not by force through the state of possessing three folds—which has been identified as being bound by a golden chain—this constitutes *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy of result), where the holding of the breasts by the middle part is fancied as the result [of that identification]; since this is established [as a fact], it is a case where the object [of the fancy] is established (*siddhaviṣayā*).

Since the attainment of union with the feet of a beloved woman is not the actual fruit of the water-lily’s penance—which consists of its dwelling in the water—this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the fruit) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha*), because that [union] is fancied as the fruit of the penance, being as rare as a flower in the sky. Other examples follow this same sequence: "The young moons [of buds], curved and yet not blooming, and the exceedingly red *palāśa* flowers shone like fresh nail-marks upon the forest grounds that have just been united with Spring."

Because of the connection between the crookedness and redness of the *atrapalāśa* flowers and [the nails], there arises a probability of their identity with fresh nail-marks; thus, this is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature itself) where the object of the statement is explicitly mentioned. The distinction here is that in the previous example (*pūrva-udāharaṇa*), the connection with the property serving as the cause was implied (*gamya*), whereas here it is explicitly stated (*upātta*). Now, one might argue that since the word *iva* is well-known to denote similarity, this should simply be considered a simile (*upamā*).

If it is argued that—just as in the example "limpatī" (she smears), where the agent of the smearing, who is fit to be the standard of comparison, has his action made subordinate—here too there is no absence of the subordination of the nail-marks to something else which would subvert the simile—the answer is stated: since a simile could have been expressed here even with nail-marks that are merely occasional, the inclusion of the qualifier "connected with the forest site where the hero and heroine met during spring" was not required; therefore, its mention [is for a specific purpose].

The word *iva* is established in the sense of a "possibility of identity" (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*) with the nail-marks; for it is only in such a state that the qualification [by *iva*] is purposeful. And the word *iva* occurs in the sense of possibility, as in: "O Devadatta, stand there; he appears as if [he were you]. "The ocean, as if grinding the sandalwood-foam with the tips of its waves, takes it up; then the moon, as if with its rays, anoints the women of heaven. In this instance, the propelling of the sandalwood-foam by the tips of the waves is imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being the act of grinding.

The spreading of the rays of the moon risen from the ocean—first extending over the ocean's flood and then pervading the quarters—is imagined as being anointing itself with sandalwood paste made of foam from the ocean's shores. In both cases, the respective causes are the gathering of masses of foam-sandalwood at the ocean's edge and the whitening of the quarters; since the objects of the [imagined] actions—the propelling of the foam-sandalwood and the pervading [of the rays]—are not mentioned, these are instances of *svarūpotprekṣā* (intrinsic poetic fancy) where the object is unstated.

However, for those who hold the view that there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the attributes of "grinding" and "smearing" performed by the ocean and the moon themselves—both of which are appropriated [as subjects]—in their opinion, the distinction is to be understood as follows: in the previous example, there was a poetic fancy of the identity (*tādātmya*) of one subject with another subject; here, however, there is a poetic fancy of the connection (*saṃsarga*) of an attribute with the subject. [The King], possessing lordly power, created on earth majesty and fame that shine perpetually, as if because of the absence of the sun at night and the moon by day.

Although the absence of the sun at night and of the moon during the day exists, it is the cause for the production of his majesty and fame; thus, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding his being the cause of those two—though the object is already established—is a *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy based on causality). "By Vivasvat, the cows that are another name for the eyes of people were surely led away along with his own thousand cows; therefore, this blindness [of the world] is indeed due to that, and not from darkness."

Even the rays of the sun are imagined as having been created by the sun himself along with his own beams for the purpose of closing the eyes of people at night—this being the cause of their blindness; thus, this is a *hetūtprekṣā* (causal fancy) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha*). I suspect that the moon, in order to increase the flood of the ocean, milks from the moonstones how much water, and during separation from their beloveds, how much from the eyes of the sorrowful female *kokila* birds.

In this case, the swelling of the ocean caused by the moon is already an established fact; it is therefore imagined as the result of two other effects: the melting of the moonstones and the shedding of tears from the eyes of the *kokila* birds. Thus, this is a "poetic fancy regarding a result" (*phalotprekṣā*) whose object is an established fact. The sun set out toward the northern direction, the birthplace of the finest horses, as if to turn back those ancient steeds who were stationed on his chariot.

Here, the turning of the horse of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is imagined as a fruit that does not actually exist; thus, this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy of the result) with an unreal object. These alone are the [explicit] poetic fancies. As for the words enumerated as indicators of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā-vyañjaka*), such as "I think" (*manye*), "I suspect" (*śaṅke*), "certainly" (*dhruvam*), "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*), "surely" (*nūnam*), and so forth, when these are employed, the fancy is expressed (*vācyā*). When they are not employed, the fancy is implied (*gamyā*).
For example: "Your fame, weary from wandering, entered the celestial river. (33-35)
Metaphorical hyperbole (rūpakātiśayokti) occurs through the determination [of one thing] as another after having swallowed up [its own nature]; for example:
"Behold, sharp arrows are emerging from the pair of blue lotuses. (36)

The swallowing of the object (*viṣaya-nigaraṇa*) consists in the apprehension of the object by means of the word denoting the subject (*viṣayin*) alone, even without the mention of the object by its own name. When there is a superimposed certainty (*āhārya-niścaya*)—the determination of the object as having the nature of the subject—preceded by that swallowing, there is *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor). For instance, in the example [under discussion], there is first the apprehension of the eyes and the side-glances by the words "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and "arrows" (*śara*), followed by the determination of them as being of that very nature.

Or, for example: "A certain pond shines in the sky; beyond it lies a subtle path reaching a golden and sapphire staircase. Ahead are two mountains, easily accessible to the virtuous, their regions covered with sandalwood; there, nectar is easily obtained by those dwelling there due to the proximity of the moon. Here, by the words "pond" and so forth, the navel and other parts are swallowed up [in the metaphor]. In this case, the mention of "metaphor" as a qualification of the hyperbole (atiśayokti) is intended to demonstrate by extension that the various types shown under the heading of metaphor are also possible here.

Therefore, here too, one should observe the two-fold division into *abhedātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-difference) and *tādrūpyātiśayokti* (hyperbole of identity). Furthermore, within those, the distinction between excess (*ādhikya*) and deficiency (*nyūnatā*) should be kept in mind throughout. Or, for example: "Followed by the cakora birds of your speech, who have taken a mouthful of nectar, casting forth a pure moonlight that possesses the ripeness of the lavalī fruit—cast your eyes toward the top of the rampart of the simile and consider: what is this cool-rayed moon in the sky of your face, from which the deer has vanished?"

In this passage, by the statement “What is this cool-rayed one whose deer has vanished?”, the distinction from the well-known moon and his superiority over it are both implied. In other cases as well, it should be inferred in the same way. ||36||
If it possesses the nature of being pregnant with a concealment, that very [speech] is considered "with concealment" (sapahnavā);
thus, through the delusion that it is nectar, people perceive your excellent verses as such even in the moon. 37.

In this instance, the hyperbole (atiśayokti) stating that "the sweetness of your eloquent speech alone is nectar" contains within it a concealment (apahnuti), as it implies that the nectar residing in the lunar orb is not [actual] nectar. Or, for example: "The sweet juice is between the pearl and the coral; the supreme flower-bearer resides in the orb of the moon; their coexistence is indeed not in the ocean. It rises upon the crest of the conch, but not within the Eastern Mountain—these are the things they imagine, for those whose eyes have never beheld her."

Here, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form "the lower nectar is indeed the honeyed nectar," which contains within it an *apahnuti* (concealment), as it implies that the nectar of flowers is not truly the honeyed nectar. However, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has cited this as an example of *sāpahnavā svarūpotprekṣā* (a conceit of essential nature involving concealment): "When the city's playful women hurriedly retreated to the bank due to the collisions with sea-monsters, there the Śiprā river shone as if laughing with loud bursts of pearls under the guise of its rising mass of foam. The difference here, however, is this: the present case contains a pure *apahnuti* within it.

In that case, where the state of being a mass of foam is denied, there is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of it being a loud laugh; however, here, the nature of being pregnant with an inverted denial (*paryastāpahnuti*) arises because the nectar and so forth—which have been denied in the lunar orb and other such things—are established in the form of eloquent speech and the like. This quality of being pregnant with an inverted denial is also possible within a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Regarding that, as an example of a fancy concerning essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*): "I know that this very thing is the bimba fruit due to its excessive redness, and the inferiority of the [real] bimba fruit is clearly evident from this."

People, unable to perceive the distinction between the two, fell into a confusion regarding their names. Here, by means of the cause of "excessive redness" (*atirāga*), there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding Damayantī’s lip, which denies the quality of being a "Bimba fruit" (*bimbatā*) to the well-known Bimba fruit; this fancy contains within it a "converse denial" (*paryastāpahnuti*). The inclusion of such a denial within a "poetic fancy based on a cause" (*hetūtprekṣā*) is seen precisely in the previously cited example of *hetūtprekṣā*. In that case, having denied the status of being a cause of blindness to darkness itself, that causality was attributed elsewhere.

An example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) is as follows: "Surely the elephant, scorched by the sun, enters the lake to harass the lotuses that are its [natural] enemies, and not to bathe; for the bathing of an elephant is never fruitless. Here, with respect to the elephant’s entry into the lake, the status of "result" (*phalatva*) belonging to bathing is denied and attributed instead to the harassing of the lotuses. Enough of this digression; let us return to our main subject. (37)
Exaggeration by way of distinction (bhedakātiśayokti), however, is the description of that very thing as being something else:
"The profundity of this lord of the earth is one thing, his fortitude is another. (38)
In this case, although there is no difference in the depth and other qualities well-known in the world, a distinction is described:
"This perfection of form is one thing, and this flow of cleverness is another; this lotus-petal-eyed maiden is not an ordinary creation of the Creator. (38)
Exaggeration of relation (*sambandhātiśayokti*) consists in the conceptualization of a connection where none exists:
"The tops of the palaces of this city touch the orb of the moon. (39)

Or, for example: "The female ruddy goose (cakravākī) experiences joy, thinking, 'In just a few days, the Golden Mountain (Mahāmeru), which brings the day to its close, will come to an end,' while King Vīrarudradeva is characterized by his liberality. Here, although there is no actual connection between the female ruddy goose's satisfaction and the destruction of Mount Meru—which causes the sun to set—the connection is described as such. (39)
Even when there is a connection, the absence of that connection is called the hyperbole of non-connection (*asaṃbandhātiśayokti*).
"O Indra among kings! Since you are the giver, we do not hold the celestial trees in high regard. (40)

Here, although there is no connection between the celestial tree (the wish-fulfilling tree) and the longing, their connection is described; thus, this is the figure of speech *asaṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection). Or, for example: "O lady of faultless limbs! As these two breasts of yours expand, there is not enough space within the expanse of your arms. (40)
There may be the figure of speech called *akrama-atiśayokti* (simultaneity-exaggeration) when cause and effect are perceived as occurring together;
"O King! Your arrows and your enemies embrace the bowstring at the same time. (41)

In this case, the simultaneity (*sahatva*) of cause and effect is described: at the very moment the stringing of the arrow with the bowstring is performed, the enemies fall to the ground. Or, for example: "The host of enemies releases [their wealth], releases it; they abandon their treasury, abandon it; they suffer trembling, they suffer it; and they quickly abandon patience, they abandon it—[all] upon the sword of the Hammīra hero being drawn from its sheath. Here, at the very time the sword leaves its sheath and so forth, the enemies' abandonment of their treasuries and the like is described. (41)
The hyperbole of transference (*capalātiśayokti*) occurs when the cause is attributed to the effect;
for instance, when the slender lady said, "I am going," her bracelets became rings. (42)

Here, the extreme emaciation of the woman is shown by way of its effect, arising merely from the fact that her husband is away on a journey. Or, for example: "Even when a flower is seen but once, the fingertips redden to take it; at the mere news of dyeing with lac, the soles of the feet suddenly turn crimson; even the memory of anointing the limbs brings extreme distress; alas, for the woman of unsteady gaze, what else remains? Even the fragrance of her hair becomes a burden. Or, for example: "When the husband says before her, 'Shall I go? or 'Shall I not go?', in an instant the bracelets of the slender-limbed woman slip off, and likewise, other [ornaments] break apart. (42)
Exaggeration by absolute excess (atyantātiśayokti), however, occurs when there is a reversal of the sequence [of cause and effect]:
"O beloved, her pride departed first, and afterwards she was conciliated by him. (43)

"Extreme hyperbole (*atyantātiśayokti*), however, arises when the cause is attributed to the effect, as in: 'When the slender maiden uttered, "I shall go," her bracelets became rings. Or, for example: "O King, the courtyards of the lords of poets were first filled with the sweet fragrance of the rut of elephants, agitated by the contact of wandering bees; afterwards, the glances of King Rudra fell upon them—glances that were companions to the vast waves surging from the Ocean of Milk. These three types of hyperbole are intended to convey the swiftness of the effect. (43)
Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing) is the unity of attributes between those subjects being described and others; for example:
"The lotuses close, as do the faces of unchaste women. (44)
When the softness of your limbs is beheld, in whose heart does the hardness of the *mālatī*, the moon, the *sahakāra* mango, the *bhṛllekhā* jasmine, and the plantain not appear? (45)

*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is the connection of a single attribute—whether a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a form (*rūpa*)—among subjects that are either relevant (*prastuta*) or irrelevant (*aprastuta*). "They contract" is an example of *tulyayogitā* involving relevant subjects. Therein, the connection of the single action of "contracting" is shown between the lotuses—which are the subjects of description as effects of the rising moon—and the faces of wanton women who fear the light. In the following verse, while the tenderness of the heroine is the relevant subject of description, there is a connection with the single quality of being "extremely hard" among irrelevant subjects such as the *mālatī* jasmine and others.

Or rather, just as days that possess a profusion of newly sprouted leaves and lotuses—having attained a state of vivid crimson through the touch of the sun’s rays—reach their full development upon blooming; so too, the trunks of lordly elephants, due to the roughness of their skin, and the finest plantain trees, due to their extreme coolness, though they attain a vast circumference in the world, must be excluded from being compared to her thighs.

Here, in the description of summer, there is a connection with a single action between the days and the lotuses presented as being related to it; and in the description of the thighs, there is a connection with a single quality between the elephant trunks and the special plantain trees which are not the subject at hand. (44–45)
Another form of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) consists in the equality of treatment toward both the beneficial and the harmful:
"Both friend and enemy are dealt with defeat by you. (46)

In this instance, there is equality of function (*vṛttitulyatva*) because of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) through *śleṣa* (punning) of the beneficial and the harmful, and of the friend and the enemy, with respect to the granting of supreme prosperity and the granting of defeat. Or, for example: "Whether one cuts the neem tree with an axe, or treats it with honey and clarified butter, or honors it with perfumes, garlands, and the like—it remains bitter to everyone."

In this case, the sentences are to be completed by supplying the verbs *vṛścati* (cuts), *siñcati* (sprinkles), and *arcati* (worships). The distinction is that while the previous example culminates in praise, this one culminates in censure. This is the *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) as described in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*. 46.
Equalizing speech regarding those distinguished by their qualities is another [figure], *tulyayogitā* (equal conjunction):
"Yama, the world-protector; Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose; Kubera, the giver of wealth; and you, O Śakra as well. (47)

In this instance, the king being described is equated with Śakra and the other world-protectors. Or, for example: "The glances of deer-eyed women, even when initiated by wealth, do not remain for even two moments, just like flashes of lightning. In the former case there is praise; here, however, there is censure. This has been shown in the *Kāvyādarśa*. Some have designated this *tulyayogitā* as *siddhi*, as Jayadeva said: "When a name is mentioned among the well-known for the sake of expressing equality, it is *siddhi*."

"Only you two are renowned here; you are like an ocean by your forces, as the ocean is by its waters. In other systems, this is considered merely a *dīpaka* (illuminator) which will be discussed hereafter. ||47||
The wise define *dīpaka* as the unification of the attributes of things that are both described and not described; for example:
"The young elephant shines with rut, and the lord of the earth shines with his majesty. (48)

The *dīpaka* (illuminator) is the connection of a single attribute among both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*). For example, the connection of the action of "perceiving" between the relevant elephant-cub and the irrelevant king; or as in: "A gem polished on a whetstone, a victor in battle crushed by weapons, an elephant whose rut has faded, rivers in autumn with their sandy banks exposed, the moon with but a sliver remaining, a young woman exhausted by lovemaking—all these shine with a certain thinness: the gem when its brilliance has vanished, the victor when his wealth is lost, the elephant when his strength is gone, the river when its water has ebbed, the moon when it is near waning, and the woman when her pride is spent; even so do kings shine when they have lost their power to supplicants. In this verse, the quality of "shining with thinness" (*tanimnā śobhante*) connects the relevant objects (the gem, the victor, etc. with the irrelevant ones (the rivers, the moon, the woman), thereby functioning as a *dīpaka*.

Here, there is a connection with the single common attribute of "beauty" (śobhā) between the subjects under discussion—the kings—and the non-subjects—the jewels and so forth. A common attribute residing primarily in the subject incidentally benefits others, just as a lamp placed for the purpose of illuminating a palace also lights up the street; because of this similarity to a lamp, it is called *dīpaka*. The suffix *kan* is added in the sense of "light" (*diva*) according to the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ ca*. Although it is said: "Three kinds of men gather the golden flowers of the earth: the brave, the learned, and he who knows how to serve."

In this [example], the simultaneous connection of the attributes of both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*) appears. In the verse "The young elephant shines with rut," the connection of the attribute belongs first to the irrelevant [subject] alone; nevertheless, its status as a *prasaṅga* (incidental or contextual) description is not lost, because the description—which proceeds by way of the relevant subject—actually connects with the primary irrelevant [subject] in reality.

For the lamp does not lose its incidental nature (prāsaṅgikatva) by simultaneously benefiting both the street and the palace, nor does the soup cooked for the son-in-law lose its incidental nature by being served first to the guests; however, the distinction in *tulyayogitā* is that while one subject is relevant (*prastuta*) and the other is irrelevant (*aprastuta*), there is no apprehension of such a distinction, and thus the connection with the attribute occurs with reference to all subjects alike.

Furthermore, this is another distinction between these two: although there is no difference in both cases regarding the fact that the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) is implied (*gamya*), here the relationship of subject (*upameya*) and object (*upamāna*) is fixed, such that the non-contextual element is the *upamāna* and the contextual element is the *upameya*; whereas in the other case, because no such distinction is perceived, that relationship is arbitrary. 48.
When there is a repetition of three kinds [of elements] in the *dīpaka* figure, it becomes *āvṛttidīpaka* (repeated *dīpaka*).
For example: "This garland of clouds is raining, and this night is also raining. (49)
The kadamba flowers are blossoming, the emerging kuṭaja blooms are opening, the cātaka birds are intoxicated with joy, and the peacocks are likewise enraptured. (50)

Because it serves multiple purposes like a lamp (*dīpaka*), the *āvṛtti-dīpaka* (repetition-lamp) occurs when there is a repetition of the word standing in the place of the lamp, its meaning, or both; it is of three kinds. Examples are shown in sequence by three half-verses: Or, for example: "The garland of clouds excites the flock of peacocks, and today the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) excites the hearts of the youths. The stream from the rain-clouds quenches the long-standing thirst of the young *cātaka* birds. In this case, the single word *utkaṇṭhayati* ("excites") and *śamayati* ("quenches") are repeated with different meanings. Thus, it is an instance of *āvṛtti-dīpaka*.

And the stream of water from the bride’s eyes extinguishes the passion of lovers for the rainy season. O beautiful one, the orb of the moon, defeated by your face, hides within the cloud; and the lotus, too, O lovely lady, hides within the flood of waters. Thus, even though these instances of *āvṛtti* (repetition) lack the quality of having both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*) as their objects, they are designated as *dīpaka* (the Illuminator) merely because they possess the shadow or appearance of *dīpaka*. 49–50.
When there is a single commonality between two statements, it is considered *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism):
"The sun shines with its heat; the hero shines with his bow. (51)

*Prativastūpamā* (Parallel Simile) occurs where a single common attribute is stated separately in two distinct sentences—the one containing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the other the object of comparison (*upameya*). This is based on the etymological derivation: "that in which there is a simile (*upamā*) as a common attribute for every subject matter (*prati-vastu*, i.e., for every sentence-meaning). For example, in this very instance, the single attribute "shines" (*bhrājate*) and "is resplendent" (*rājate*) is indicated by two separate words in the two sentences concerning the standard and the object of comparison. Or, for example: "The firm character of the virtuous is not subverted by the intellect of the wicked."

For the flame of a jewel-lamp is not extinguished even by a gale; or rather, how could one who has fixed his soul upon your lotus-feet, which distill nectar, desire anything else? When a lotus abounds with honey, the bee does not look toward the juice of the sugarcane.

In this instance, although a difference in attributes appears—namely, "non-willing" (*anicchā*) in the sentence concerning the object of comparison (*upameya*) and "not looking" (*avīkṣā*) in the sentence concerning the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—nevertheless, since mere looking, being something to be disregarded, cannot be the object of prohibition, this prohibition of looking preceded by a desire results ultimately in "non-willing. Thus, the identity of the attribute (*dharmaikya*) should be understood. The distinction is that *arthāvṛttidīpaka* concerns either only relevant (*prastuta*) or only irrelevant (*aprastuta*) things, whereas *prativastūpamā* concerns both relevant and irrelevant things.

Moreover, this is another distinction: *āvṛttidīpaka* (repeated illuminator) is not possible through contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), whereas *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) is seen even through contrast. For example: "Only the learned man knows the toil of the learned; for a barren woman does not know the heavy pains of childbirth. "If men possess virtues, they blossom forth of their own accord; for the fragrance of musk is not made manifest by an oath. (51)
If the relationship between an object and its reflection is the illustration, then that is the poetic figure (dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra):
"O King, you alone possess fame; for the moon alone possesses splendor. (52)

Where two distinct attributes in the sentences of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are presented in the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), that is *dṛṣṭānta* (the Exemplification). In the example, “You alone are possessed of fame,” there is the relationship of original image and reflection between fame (*kīrti*) and luster (*kānti*). Or, for instance: “O King, let there be thousands of other kings as you wish; they say this earth is truly ‘possessed of a king’ because of you. Though crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, the night is radiant only by means of the moon.”

Or, for example: "Indeed, many worship the goddess of speech, yet it is only this poet Murāri—who has undergone the hardships of the preceptor’s household—that thoroughly knows its essence. The ocean was indeed crossed by the monkey-heroes, but only Mount Mandara, whose massive body is submerged in the depths of the underworld, knows its profound depth. [Objection: In this case, since the attribute of "knowledge" is the same in both the sentence concerning the object of comparison and the sentence concerning the subject of comparison, a *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) would be more appropriate.

Not so; for since consciousness is impossible in the insentient Mount Manthācala, the phrase "he knows" (jānāti) there intends merely the contact [of the mountain] with the region as far as the bottom of the ocean. In this example, the distinction from the *dīpaka* based on the repetition of words (*padāvṛtti-dīpaka*) should be understood as being, as before, caused by the subject matter being both relevant and irrelevant. This [figure] is also seen through contrast (*vaidharmya*): "You have set your mind toward pride; what else [could happen]? Thus our enemies have been struck down.
For darkness persists only so long as the sun does not reach the crest of the mountain of sunrise. (52)
*Nidarśanā* (Illustration) is the superimposition of identity between two similar sentence-meanings:
"That gentleness of the donor is the very spotlessness of the full moon. (53)

In this instance, there is an imposition of identity (*aikyāropa*) between the meaning of the sentence containing the object of comparison—the mildness of the donor—and the meaning of the sentence containing the standard of comparison—the spotlessness of the full moon—by means of the words *yat* and *tat*. Or, for example: "A cry has been wailed in the wilderness; a corpse has been anointed with unguents; a lotus has been planted on dry land and watered for a long time in barren soil; a dog’s tail has been bent down; whispered prayers have been offered into the ears of the deaf; a mirror has been held before the face of the blind: all this was done because a foolish person was served."
Here, there is a superimposition of identity between the service of ignorant people and such acts as weeping in the forest. ||53||
Some also state that the simile (nidarśanā) consists in the occurrence of the meanings of the words [in the same relation];
"That pair of eyes bears the likeness of two blue lotuses. (54)

Here, in the pair of eyes, there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), consisting of the superimposition of the property of a blue lotus upon them. Or, for example: "The paleness that was seen on the surface of the cheeks of the women of Gauḍa during separation was found in the pollen within the clusters of the date-palm blossoms. The distinction between these two examples is that in the former, a property of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is superimposed upon the subject of comparison (*upameya*), whereas here, a property of the subject of comparison is superimposed upon the object of comparison. In both cases, however, because a property belonging to one thing cannot reside in another, it implies a similar property; thus, the ultimate result is the same: the establishment of a simile.

This is called *lalitopamā* (graceful simile) by Jayadeva; it is an instance of *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* (illustration based on the meaning of individual words). Although the verse beginning with "In separation from Gauḍa women... (*viyoge gauḍanārīṇām*) has been cited by earlier authorities as an example of *vākyārthavṛttinidarśanā* (illustration based on the meaning of the entire sentence), we have cited it here by following this distinction: *vākyārthavṛttinidarśanā* consists in the superimposition of identity between two specific attributes, whereas *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* consists in the superimposition of the attributes of one object upon the other, whether that object be the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object compared (*upameya*).

And thus, in such instances as: “O Śiva, while you, the giver, exist, we follow another [cow], imitating the mudrā of purpose, desiring to milk that which is difficult to grasp with our feet, even though the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) stands before us. and: “Desiring to cross the ocean with two sticks, they praised the ocean, which is a sea of virtues,” and so forth—even though there is no difference in the syntactical structure (*vākyabheda*)—the figure of speech is indeed *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile), because of the presence of the superimposition of identity between two distinct entities.

In the defining statement, "of two sentence-meanings that are similar," the term *vākyārtha* (sentence-meaning) is intended to refer to two properties—one contextual and one non-contextual—characterized by their respective subjects which stand in the relation of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). Thus, in the example: "Service to kings for men is like licking the edge of a sword, embracing a lion, or kissing the mouth of a female serpent," there is no deficiency in this as an instance of *vākyārthavṛtti-nidarśanā* (illustration based on the meaning of a sentence), even though the individual occurrences of the contextual and non-contextual events are conveyed by single words.

This is because those two consist of a linguistic usage characterized by entities that have entered into a relationship of original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*). For this very reason, there is a distinction between *nidarśanā* and *rūpaka*. In *rūpaka*, there is indeed a superimposition of identity between two things—such as a face and the moon—that are not [previously] qualified [by such a relationship]. "The pillar-like foot of Hari was raised upward during the subduing of Bali..."

"May the stalk of the lotus that serves as the seat of the Creator be for your delight! Even in this example of *viśiṣṭarūpaka* (qualified metaphor), there is no occurrence of the relation between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), because the inclusion of those qualifiers is solely for the purpose of establishing the possession of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) consisting in being qualified by the stalk of the lotus-seat of the Creator. This is unlike examples of *nidarśana* (illustrative simile) such as "that gentleness of the Giver," where the Giver, the full moon, and so forth possess the status of the original object (*bimba*) through their shared quality of producing bliss, and thus the two qualifiers stand in a relationship of mutual reflection.

However, where there exists a relationship of original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*) due to mutual similarity between the object, the subject, and their qualifiers—as in this example of a *sāvayava-rūpaka* (compound metaphor): “Night, this female mendicant (*kāpālikī*), white with the smearing of moonlight-ashes, bearing the stars as her bones, and delighting in the passion for disappearance, wanders from island to island, carrying in the skull-bowl of the moon the fragrance of the magical ointment (*siddhāñjana*) placed within it under the guise of its dark spot. In this instance, the mutual similarity between the object, the subject, and their respective qualifiers establishes the relationship of original and reflection.

In that case as well, there is a superimposition of identity only between each individual pair of the object and the subject, along with their respective qualifiers; however, there is no superimposition of identity in the form of the qualified whole between the object in the form of a night characterized by moonlight and the subject in the form of a female Ākāpālikī characterized by ashes and so forth. Therefore, even in instances such as "Service to kings [is like service to serpents] for men," it is appropriate to regard it only as *nidarśanā* (illustration) occurring at the level of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). According to other schools of thought, however, in this instance it must be considered *nidarśanā* occurring at the level of the word-meaning (*padārtha*). ||54||
