They say that another means of awakening consists in the demonstration of the non-existence and existence of things through action:
"The opponent of the king shall perish," just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the moon. (55)
Even as he rises, the sun bestows splendor upon our homes;
manifesting the fruit of prosperity, he is the benefactor of his friends. (56)

When something belonging to someone who is distinguished by a particular action is described as communicating—through its own action—to others an object that is either non-existent or existent, that is called *aparanidarśanā*. For the communication of a non-existent object, the second half-verse serves as the illustration.

In this context, although one could have said "it would perish while making [the king] aware," the word "making aware" (*bodhayat*) is not used because its meaning is already implied. Thus, darkness—being opposed to King Candra—is itself characterized by the act of perishing; and by means of its own act of perishing, which serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it conveys the sense that ends in an undesirable consequence: "If anyone else is opposed to the king, they too should perish. Because the meaning is based on the fact that [darkness] has perished while conveying this sense, this is an instance of *asadarthanidarśanā* (illustration with an unreal object).

Similarly, in the following verse, the Sun, bestowing Lakṣmī upon the lotuses at the very moment of his rising, is composed as an *udāharaṇa* (illustrative example) of a beneficial truth: by the act of conferring the beauty of the lotus upon others, he demonstrates that the fruit of prosperity for others is indeed the favoring of friends. Or, for example: "Proclaiming that 'he who has attained a high position, being light [in character], will surely fall with ease,' the speck of dust situated upon the crest of a mountain peak falls downward, shaken by the beautiful breeze."

Here, a cluster of raindrops situated on the peak of a mountain, shaken even by a gentle breeze, falls; this is composed as an illustration of an unreal thing (*asadarthanidarśanā*), teaching the false principle that the very cause of one's fall is the attainment of a high position for the light-minded. [And: "He who places the Sun-god, when he has arrived, in the position of his crest-jewel, should offer hospitality to the virtuous"—this [verse] is composed to inform householders.

Here, by honoring with his head the sun that has arrived at dawn through the act of holding up his own spittle, the poet conveys the true meaning (*sad-artha*) that householders should offer hospitality (*ātithya*) to those who arrive in this manner; thus, it is an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) based on an illustration of a true fact. Regarding this, some maintain that there are two types of *nidarśanā*: one occurring at the level of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-vṛtti*) and one occurring at the level of the word-meaning (*padārtha-vṛtti*), both of which are based on the connection of an impossible thing, whereas the third type is based on the connection of a possible thing. This is how they distinguish them.

For instance, in the first illustration, the identity between the sentence and its meaning is impossible, and thus it results in their similarity. In the third illustration, however, the communication of true or false matters to others by means of one's own action—which is indeed possible—implicitly contains the notion of equality.

For in such instances as “awakening the householders,” the fire made of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣo’gniḥ*) renders students capable of study by removing the cold; described in this manner, the mountain is able, by its very nature as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), to make the householders capable of the aforementioned awakening. Just as this mountain honors the approaching sun with its head, so too should the householder honor the one who has arrived with appropriate worship. Therefore, a connection with awakening is possible. (55–56)
